name: QLab
subcategory: live show control and cue playback
tagline: macOS show control for theatre and live events: audio, video, lighting and MIDI cues fired from one cue list.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Licensing is per machine with both purchase and short-term rental options, so a monthly figure does not map cleanly.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build a cue list that plays sound files when you hit the space bar, and for a school play with four sound effects that is genuinely enough. What you cannot one-shot is the part that matters: a real-time playback engine that does not glitch, drop a frame, or crash in front of 400 paying people, driving a 16 channel interface, two projectors, DMX fixtures, MIDI to the lighting desk and timecode out, all while a stage manager improvises around a missed entrance. QLab's actual product is twenty years of edge cases in that specific environment plus the fact that every designer and venue tech already knows the keyboard shortcuts and can open your workspace file cold. A personal replacement has no second operator, no rental licence for tech week, no venue that trusts it. Build the toy player for your own living room installation, not for anything with an audience and a ticket price.
coreLoopDIY: A local macOS app with an ordered cue list that fires audio files on a GO key, with per-cue volume, fade in and out, loop, and selectable output device.
requirements: an audio interface if you want more than stereo out
a spare keyboard or USB footswitch if you want a dedicated GO key
whatYouLose: Video, lighting and DMX, MIDI, OSC and timecode cues, which is most of what QLab actually is
Real-time reliability under load: QLab is engineered so a show does not die mid-cue, and your weekend build is not
Multi-channel routing, matrix mixing, per-output levels and device hot-swap handling
Portability between operators and venues: nobody else can open or run your file, and no house tech will touch it
Rental licences, crash recovery, versioned workspaces and a support channel that answers during tech week
moatNotes: The trust here is unusually literal: the failure mode is a silent theatre and a visible human taking the blame, so nobody experiments on opening night.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the cost of a glitch is public and immediate, and because QLab is the lingua franca of live show control. A sound designer hands a workspace to a venue and the venue knows exactly what to do with it. The money is not buying a file player, it is buying the assumption that it will survive 30 performances, plus the hardware integration work nobody wants to debug at 2am during tech. Even people who could write their own cue player do not, because the thing they would be writing is reliability, not features.
notes: A keyboard-triggered sound player is a weekend; a show that never fails is not. The moat is two decades of live-event edge cases plus the fact that every designer and venue tech already speaks QLab.
prompt:
Build a minimal local audio cue player for macOS. Native app, no web stack.

Stack: Swift, SwiftUI, AVFoundation (AVAudioEngine plus AVAudioPlayerNode). Xcode project, single window, macOS 13 or later. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics, no network calls at all.

Core model: a Workspace is an ordered list of Cues saved as a single JSON file the user picks (document-based or simple open/save to a chosen path). A Cue has: number (string), name, audio file path, start time offset, volume in dB, fade in seconds, fade out seconds, loop bool, and a post-wait plus auto-continue flag.

UI: left pane is the cue list as a table with number, name, file name, duration, and a live elapsed/remaining readout for anything playing. Right pane is an inspector for the selected cue with the fields above. Bottom bar has GO, Stop All, and a master fade-out slider. Playing cues show a progress bar in the row.

Keys: space is GO and fires the selected cue then advances the playhead to the next cue. Escape is panic stop all with a 0.3s fade. Up and down arrows move the playhead without firing. Make the GO key mapping a constant in one place.

Audio: preload decoded buffers for every cue file when the workspace opens so GO latency is low, and show a loading indicator while that happens. Support wav, aiff, mp3, m4a. Allow multiple cues playing at once, mixed through one AVAudioEngine. Implement fades with a ramp on the player node volume, not by re-rendering audio. Let the user pick an output device from a popup and handle the device disappearing without crashing.

Explicitly out of scope: video, images, lighting, DMX, MIDI, OSC, timecode, network control, multi-channel matrix routing, cue carts, groups, scripts, and any remote app.

On first launch open an empty untitled workspace. Dragging audio files onto the cue list appends cues with sensible defaults. Write a README that states plainly this is a personal tool, that it has not been tested under live show conditions, and that anyone running an actual ticketed performance should use QLab.
